evidence.quote: The core operation — deciding whether a passage satisfies a requirement written in different words — is a semantic judgement over natural language. Rule-based matching and keyword search cannot recognise that "our ISO 27001-certified information security management system" satisfies "the supplier must maintain a recognised information security framework".

The proposal therefore uses GenAI only where semantic judgement is required, and surrounds it with deterministic verification: quotations must exist in the source, every requirement must receive a decision with evidence or an explicit "not found", and the human reviewer decides.

For each requirement the assessment agent receives the requirement text and the eight best candidate passages, each with an identifier. It must return JSON with status (addressed | partial | not_found), quotes (each with passage identifier and verbatim text) and rationale.

The system has six components (Appendix A): a document parser (PyMuPDF), a requirement extractor (LLM with structured output, followed by human correction), a hybrid retriever (BM25 (Robertson & Zaragoza, 2009) plus dense embeddings with reciprocal-rank fusion), an assessment agent, a verifier, and a review interface (FastAPI back end, React front end, SQLite store).

The verifier checks that each quotation is a substring of the identified passage after whitespace normalisation; failing quotations are removed, and a finding left with no valid quotation is downgraded to not found — needs manual check.

TenderLens is a local web application. A panel member uploads the RFT and a response, reviews the extracted requirement register, starts the check, and receives an evidence matrix: one row per requirement, with a status, one to three quotations, their page locations and a short rationale.

Development uses a hosted model through an OpenAI-compatible interface at temperature 0. We will compare one frontier model and one smaller open-weight model on the development set and select on macro-F1 and cost.
If behind schedule, we de-scope in this order: FR15 comparison, FR6 export formatting, the second model comparison.

It (1) extracts a structured requirement register from the RFT, (2) parses each supplier response while preserving page and section locations, (3) locates candidate evidence for each requirement, (4) asks a language model to classify each requirement as addressed, partially addressed or not found with verbatim quotations, (5) verifies every quotation against the source document and (6) presents an evidence matrix that the panel member confirms or overrides. Every finding links to the exact page and paragraph it relies on.

The proposal therefore uses GenAI only where semantic judgement is required, and surrounds it with deterministic verification: quotations must exist in the source, every requirement must receive a decision with evidence or an explicit "not found", and the human reviewer decides.

Three principles from computing education research shape the design. First, productive struggle: novices learn more when they work through a difficulty with appropriate support than when they are shown the answer, provided the struggle does not tip into disengagement. Second, graded assistance: effective tutors start with the least help that might work — a question that redirects attention — and add detail only when needed.

evidence.quote: Three principles from computing education research shape the design. First, productive struggle: novices learn more when they work through a difficulty with appropriate support than when they are shown the answer, provided the struggle does not tip into disengagement. Second, graded assistance: effective tutors start with the least help that might work — a question that redirects attention — and add detail only when needed. Third, error-message literacy: many novice difficulties are not conceptual but interpretive; the student does not know what the error message is telling them (Becker et al., 2019). Enhanced explanations of error messages generated by language models have been shown to be understandable to novices in many cases, although quality varies (Leinonen et al., 2023).

The proposal is generally understandable, logically structured, and professionally written, with useful tables and a credible reference list whose in-text citations are mostly connected to relevant claims. evidence.quote: The pipeline works like this. First the transcript is parsed into utterances with ids and speaker labels and identifiers are masked by a combination of regular expressions (Medicare numbers, dates) and a named entity model for names, masked tokens are kept consistent so the note still reads correctly and they are unmasked only at display time locally. Second the drafting step sends the masked transcript to the LLM with instructions to produce a JSON object with four sections each containing a list of statements and for each statement the list of utterance ids that support it, the prompt includes the SOAP definitions and two worked examples from synthetic consults. Third the linker validates that every utterance id exists, any statement with no existing id is marked unlinked. Fourth the verifier takes each statement and its linked utterances and asks a second model call, with a different prompt and no access to the rest of the draft, whether the utterances entail the statement, contradict it or are insufficient, the answer is one of three labels, statements labelled insufficient or contradicted are flagged.

We will write 120 synthetic safety reports covering two fictional sites over four weeks, based on public examples of hazard report templates. Into these we will plant 15 recurring hazard patterns (for example, the same missing edge protection reported on different days with different wording) and 5 escalation patterns (a near miss followed by a related incident). Two team members will label each report with hazard type and the pattern it belongs to.

A team member acting as a safety manager will read each synthetic week of reports and write a briefing manually. We will also compare with a simple keyword-grouping baseline that clusters reports sharing hazard keywords.

Safety reporting on construction sites is largely free text. Supervisors write in their own words, often quickly and with site jargon ("edge pro missing on L3", "EWP near overheads"). Reports are submitted through forms or as PDFs and stored in a document system. Safety managers read them, follow up individual issues and prepare monthly summaries for management.
